critic_notes.rationale: The expression is internally consistent (the gate correctly keeps the cheap/low-growth and expensive/high-growth quadrants with the right signs), but the economics is a direct rediscovery of the well-documented book-to-market × asset-growth (HML/CMA) double sort, with the concordance gate adding construction complexity rather than a new mechanism.

Cleanly built and sign-consistent, but "cheap on cash-flow yield plus low capex intensity" simply stacks two canonical anomalies (CF/P value and the investment/capex-intensity effect) and duplicates the economic content of the other value-plus-low-investment proposals in this batch.

Dividing EBITDA yield by a small, often near-zero smoothed capex ratio makes the signal mechanically dominated by 1/capex rather than by valuation, so despite winsorization the construct is an unstable restatement of the low-investment anomaly rather than a genuine value–investment interaction.

Internally consistent, but the triple conjunction of high price-to-sales, high asset growth, and high equity issuance is essentially the published external-financing/composite-issuance and asset-growth anomaly complex, and reliance on sstk further degrades coverage without adding a distinct mechanism.

The value-conditional-on-inventory-deceleration interaction is a reasonably distinct mechanism and the gated z-score is coherently signed (ungated firms park at the industry mean), though the second-difference ACCEL term is noisy and the effective signal is a half-sample sales-yield sort.

Conditioning EBITDA yield on sales growth net of headcount growth is a genuinely non-obvious pairing of value with labor-productivity scaling rather than another value-plus-low-capex restatement, with the main caveat that emp-based growth will trim coverage and should be checked as a diagnostic.

A structurally genuine (not cosmetic) recasting of the archived Scalable Labor Value from a MIN-intersection to a gated valuation spread, with a coherent diagnosis of why the prior short tail diluted alpha, though the underlying ingredients remain plain EBITDA-yield value and the zero-masking of roughly half the cross-section will mechanically depress the Fama-MacBeth slope even if the conditioning is real.

This is a mechanical recombination of two already-evaluated archive constructs — the inventory-reset leg (ACCEL→DELTA is a minor smoothing swap) inserted into the SUB(MIN,MIN) quadrant template that already delivered a significantly *negative* FF5 alpha — and the inventory-intensity leg is close to the published inventory-growth/change anomaly (Thomas–Zhang, Belo–Lin) interacted with value.

The diagnosis that the archived stability spread's negative alpha came from a badly constructed short leg is credible and the gated version is a substantively different portfolio construction, but it reuses the same INDICATOR-gate template as the first proposal in this batch, so the two are partly redundant tests of one idea.

The discipline leg, capx/at minus asset growth, is dominated by the negative of the well-documented asset-growth anomaly (Cooper–Gulen–Schill) crossed with value, and its high tail — heavy capex alongside shrinking total assets — is as likely to select asset-shedding or distressed firms as "disciplined maintenance," which contradicts the stated economic reading.

Internally consistent and the net-liquidity-change leg is a genuinely different capital-allocation measure from the capex/inventory legs already tested, though it sits close to the published net-debt-issuance / external-financing anomaly and should be checked for whether the cash-flow-yield leg is doing any incremental work.

This is the archived Priced Capacity Overhang expression with a three-period moving average wrapped around the second leg — a parameter-smoothing tweak rather than a substantively different mechanism — and the persistence argument does nothing to address why the prior version's FF5 alpha was essentially zero despite an aligned cross-sectional slope.

This is a cosmetic template swap of the archive's "Liquidity-Funded Growth Short" (same P/S × high-capex × cash-depletion mechanism, MIN-of-ranks re-expressed as the now-standard IND_ZSCORE×INDICATOR gate already used three times in the archive), so it tests no new economic content and its negative FF5 alpha is likely the same effect re-measured.

It is a single-operand substitution on the archive's best signal that replaces the asset-*age* mechanism (ppent/ppegt) with a tangibility-mix change that is largely a mechanical restatement of high capex relative to asset growth, so it dilutes rather than extends the rejuvenation story and the claimed coverage gain from dropping ppegt is marginal.

Payout is a genuinely new theme for this pair and the internally consistent free-cash-flow coverage gate (oancf − capx − dvc > 0) is a substantive sustainability condition rather than a relabeled dividend-yield sort, though the ~payer-only universe will cut coverage sharply and the result should be checked against plain dividend yield within payers.

The investment leg is a genuinely distinct construct — co-movement of capex-intensity changes with internal cash-flow changes rather than the level, growth, or volatility of investment already tested — and the NEG(ABS(...)) direction correctly matches the stated positive expected sign, with the main risk being that small mismatches proxy for firms with little activity at all.

This is essentially the published glamour-acquirer anomaly (Rau–Vermaelen 1998; Loughran–Vijh 1997) — high-valuation acquirers underperform — and the COALESCE of aqc with goodwill deltas splices two differently scaled, sparsely populated variables whose zero/missing distinction will dominate the ranking.

The non-monotonic middle-band gate is correctly constructed (the indicator difference equals 1 only for the interior band) and the ex-ante hypothesis is coherent, but a 5-observation TS_RANK places quantile values exactly on the 0.25/0.75 thresholds, making the selected band knife-edge and potentially collapsing to a thin, unstable subsample.

The expression is internally consistent and the added PP&E-scalability leg is a genuine economic tightening rather than a relabeling, but it stacks two changes at once (continuous weight plus new input) on top of the already-tested Scalable Value Gate, so any improvement will be hard to attribute.

This is a denominator tweak to the archive's already-evaluated Capital-Optionality Cash Value and the modified weight collapses toward a standard high-cash/low-leverage screen, so it is a near-duplicate whose incremental content is a well-known balance-sheet characteristic rather than a new mechanism.

Requiring a high net-to-gross PP&E ratio (which mechanically arises from recent heavy capex) jointly with low capex/ppegt is internally strained and selects a narrow, unstable subset, and the resulting value-times-low-investment tilt is largely spanned by HML and CMA in the FF5 alpha regression.

The weight is a monotone rescaling of inventory turnover, a documented efficiency anomaly, so novelty rests entirely on the interaction with cash-flow yield, but the construction is clean, industry-ranked, well-behaved at the tails, and distinct from the archive's inventory-acceleration attempt.

che/(che + accumulated depreciation) is economically and statistically close to the archive's che/(che+ppent) weight (both are dominated by cash-to-capital-intensity), making this a third member of the same cash-optionality family proposed in the same batch rather than an independent test of the replacement-burden channel.

The diagnosis of the prior change-based version's instability is credible and the bounded level measure is well-constructed and sign-coherent, though value combined with free-cash-flow coverage is close to a conventional quality-value composite and may add little beyond known FCF-yield evidence.

This is a horizon re-parameterization of the archived "Bounded Reinvestment Payback Value" (identical z-score leg, identical bounded-ratio construction, only 1-year → 3-year sales/capex windows), so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a new mechanism, and the longer window will also mechanically load on multi-year sales momentum/growth already reflected in the parent.

The expression is simply the archived "Capex-Backed Asset Renewal Value" with its capx/ppegt rank swapped for the archived "Capital-Optionality" rank che/(che+ppent), stacking two already-tested weights that both contain ppent and will therefore be highly correlated with both parents, so it offers little incremental economic content beyond mechanical recombination.

The stated safeguard fails mechanically — a large goodwill write-off simultaneously raises sale/at (smaller denominator) and lowers gdwl/at, so both legs of the MIN are jointly triggered by impairment, exactly the case the reasoning claims to exclude, and the declining-assets component overlaps the well-known asset-growth anomaly.

Reframing the capex burden as funding *uncertainty* rather than level is an economically distinct and well-motivated response to the failed bounded-coverage signal, the ratio is scale-free and monotone even for negative oancf, and it is not a known published anomaly — though a 3-observation annual VOL is a noisy volatility estimate.

The trend in sales-per-employee is a genuinely different statistic (persistent level improvement) from the archived one-year sales-minus-headcount growth gap and is motivated by the observed FMB/alpha divergence, but it remains in the same labor-productivity family and is close to the published labor-hiring/productivity literature, so the marginal novelty is modest.

This is the archived "Dual-Input Scalable Value" with emp replaced by invt, and the inventory leg duplicates the archived "Inventory-Absorption Cash Value" channel, making it a single-input substitution rather than a substantively different test.

This is a two-change recombination of the archive's Bounded Reinvestment Payback Value (Δsale→Δebitda plus oancf-yield→sale-yield anchor), and it adopts the sales-yield anchor that has already produced repeated null/negative-alpha results in this archive (Bounded Investment-Coverage 0.52/-0.034, Capex-Shock Absorption 0.10/-0.032), so the confounded design makes attribution of any result impossible.

The stated mechanism is internally inconsistent — che/(che+ppent) and sale/ppent are both mechanically decreasing in ppent, so taking their MIN amplifies rather than neutralizes the asset-lightness tilt the reasoning claims to purge, making this a low-information overlay on the already-tested Capital-Optionality Cash Value.

The diagnosis (strong FMB but weak alpha because the gross-PP&E reconciliation is contaminated by acquisitions/reclassifications) is economically coherent and the added rejuvenation requirement is a substantive verification screen, though the two gate components are partly mechanically linked since retiring fully depreciated assets by construction raises ppent/ppegt, so treat the "verification" as partial.

The multiplication of a signed price-to-sales z-score by a non-negative deterioration rank means the most extreme long positions are cheap firms with the worst dual productivity trends — the opposite of what the hypothesis describes — and the archive already shows this expensive-short composite family (Priced Capacity Overhang, Replacement-Cycle Valuation Risk) delivering conflicting FMB and FF5 evidence for exactly this structural reason.

This changes a single input (ebitda→oancf) in the already-evaluated Persistent Workforce Productivity Value and is precisely the kind of cosmetic anchor swap the objective warns against, with predictable coverage loss (~0.111→~0.08) as the main differentiator.

The bounded ratio degenerates for the large fraction of firms with zero or negative lagged inventory change, where it collapses to sign(Δoancf)=±1 and saturates the gate, so the signal mostly ranks cash-flow improvement among non-builders rather than testing whether inventory investment pays off as hypothesized.

Internally consistent and correctly signed, but it is a near-mechanical MIN merge of two already-tested archive signals whose legs share the same LAG(capx) denominator and highly collinear numerators (Δsale vs Δebitda), so the incremental economic content over "Bounded Reinvestment Payback Value" and "Operating-Profit Payback Value" is thin.

A coherent conjunction of renewal evidence and funding slack whose legs avoid the shared-denominator artifact of the earlier optionality overlay, though it remains a recombination of three previously tested legs and the che/(che+capx) term partially rewards low capex in tension with the rejuvenation requirement.

Clean, well-specified extension of the persistent-productivity family to earnings-on-installed-capital rather than turnover, with expression, sign, and hypothesis fully aligned, albeit close in spirit to the known value×profitability-trend interaction and sensitive to negative-ebitda firms in the trend.

The bounded ratio ebitda/(|ebitda|+invt) reverses its comparative statics in inventory for loss-making firms (higher inventory raises the score when ebitda<0), so the trend does not cleanly measure "working capital becoming more productive" as hypothesized, and inventory is a stock rather than the "inventory investment" the reasoning invokes.

Swapping the mechanically-related asset-age leg for an independent operating outcome is a defensible, well-motivated diagnosis of the prior signal's fmb/alpha gap, but structurally it is a one-leg substitution on an archived expression and Δ(sale/ppent) has already been used as a conditioning leg elsewhere.

Economically distinct legs (retained liquidity vs realized investment payoff) address the real concern that che/(che+ppent) may just proxy asset-lightness or underinvestment, and the conjunction is correctly signed, though it risks being dominated by the already-strong optionality leg rather than adding independent information.

This is a denominator swap on two archive signals already tested with the identical structure (Persistent Fixed-Capital Earnings Value uses TREND(ebitda/ppent) and Profitable Inventory Productivity Trend uses the same EBITDA-positivity gate with TREND(ebitda/(ebitda+invt))), so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a new mechanism.

Beyond being a third recombination of the already-tested recycling leg with the already-tested che/(che+capx) leg, the two legs pull mechanically against each other — the recycling proxy requires capx to exceed gross PP&E growth while the liquidity ratio mechanically rewards small capx — so the conjunction risks selecting low-capex disposal cases rather than the hypothesized sustainable replacement programs.

Both legs (DELTA(ppent/ppegt) rejuvenation and the bounded EBITDA-per-lagged-capex payback) have each already been tested against the same oancf-yield anchor in the archive (Rejuvenated-Asset Value Gate, Productive Renewal Value, Operating-Profit Payback Value, Payoff-Validated Capital Optionality), making this a mechanical MIN pairing of existing components with no new economic content.

This simply appends the weaker Investment-Enabled Margin Expansion leg to the fully-tested Funded Active-Investment Value expression as a third weakest-link term, which is an incremental stacking of archive components likely to shrink effective spread and coverage rather than a substantively different mechanism.

Still a conjunction of previously tested legs, but the proposal is explicitly motivated by the diagnosed FMB-strong/alpha-weak split in the total-factor family and the liquidity-coverage leg is economically distinct from productivity trends, so the test carries genuine incremental information despite three-way MIN attenuation risk.

Replacing DELTA(sale/ppent) with DELTA(oancf/ppent) in the already-evaluated Output-Verified Capital Recycling expression is a near-identical validation-leg substitution, and the cash-flow numerator additionally overlaps with the oancf-based value anchor family, so little independent evidence is expected.

MIN of a stock (che) and a flow (capx) is dimensionally incoherent and, because cash typically exceeds one year of capex for most firms, the conditioner will collapse to capx/ppegt — a renewal-intensity leg already tested in Backlog-Addressing Renewal Value and Demand-Triggered Investment Value — so it does not actually measure the "cash-covered" mechanism claimed.

Charging current capex against cash before scaling by installed capital is a substantive (not cosmetic) reformulation of the archive's strongest leg che/(che+ppent), since a material fraction of firms have capx comparable to or exceeding cash and will flip to negative net optionality, giving the signal a genuinely different cross-section.

A coherent weakest-link combination of two independently validated legs with distinct denominators and a defensible motivation (screening out passively asset-light firms), though it is incremental relative to the several existing MIN-composites and will lose coverage through emp.

Because implied retirement (capx − Δppegt) is typically an order of magnitude smaller than oancf, the MIN will almost always select the recycling term, so the expression silently discards the cash-flow-yield component the hypothesis relies on and reduces to a retirement-to-market-cap ranking dominated by gross-PP&E reconciliation noise.

Pairing asset rejuvenation with labor-productivity trend is economically sensible and avoids the shared-denominator artifact of Productive Renewal Value, but it is a modest recombination of two already-tested legs rather than a new mechanism.

This is an explicit MIN→MUL operator swap on Payoff-Validated Capital Optionality with identical economic inputs, i.e. exactly the cosmetic variant the research objective warns against, and the product of two percentile ranks will be highly correlated with their minimum.

This is a cosmetic denominator tweak to the archived Multi-Year Capex Reserve Value (adding invt to che + TS_SUM(capx,3)), which will be near-perfectly correlated with the original for most firms and offers no new economic comparative static beyond a slight re-ranking of inventory-heavy names.

This is effectively the archived Labor-Scalable Capital Optionality with the liquidity gate's denominator swapped from ppent to TS_SUM(capx,3) — two highly correlated flexibility proxies already tested against the same TREND(sale/emp) gate — so it is a variant rather than a new mechanism.

It is an intersection of two already-tested gates and therefore likely highly collinear with both, but the stated rationale identifies a real offsetting PP&E-level tilt in the two components, making it a substantive rather than purely cosmetic combination worth one test.

The design argument is coherent and non-trivial — fixed-asset turnover imposes an opposing sensitivity to PP&E scale relative to the tangible/goodwill mix — though both ingredients appear in the archive so the incremental information content may be small.

This reproduces the archived Payoff-Validated Capital Optionality with only the liquidity denominator changed from ppent to TS_SUM(capx,3), a near-substitutable flexibility scaler, so it is a cosmetic variant of an already-successful signal.

It simply stacks two gates already tested separately against the same oancf-yield base (Operating-Profit Payback and the sales-per-employee trend) with no new comparative static or offsetting mechanism to justify the intersection.
